questions.stem: The nurse is about to give an IV antibiotic through the needleless connector of a client's peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC). Which action best prevents a central line-associated bloodstream infection?

options.text: Wipe the connector briefly with a dry sterile gauze pad to remove any visible dust or residue
Scrub the connector with an alcohol or chlorhexidine pad for at least 15 seconds and let it dry
Flush the line with 10 mL of saline before cleaning it, so any bacteria are washed away
Change the needleless connector before each dose of the antibiotic so that the connector stays sterile

rationale.correct: Scrub the hub: friction with alcohol or chlorhexidine for at least 15 seconds and full drying before every access.

perOption.a: Dry gauze does not disinfect the connector.
perOption.b: Scrubbing the hub with friction and letting it dry kills organisms that could enter the line.
perOption.c: Flushing before disinfecting can push organisms into the bloodstream.
perOption.d: Connectors are changed on a set schedule, not before every dose; frequent changes add access events.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.stem: A client in an airborne infection isolation room with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis needs a chest CT scan in the radiology department. How should the nurse plan the transport?

options.text: Have the client wear an N95 respirator during transport and in the radiology department
Place a surgical mask on the client and tell radiology the client is on airborne precautions
Delay the CT scan until the client has had three negative sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli
Transport the client without a mask, since the scanning room has its own ventilation

rationale.correct: Clients on airborne precautions leave the room only when necessary, wearing a surgical mask, with the receiving department notified.

perOption.a: N95 respirators protect the wearer from inhaling particles; for the client, a surgical mask is used to contain their droplets.
perOption.b: A surgical mask on the client contains respiratory particles, and notifying the department lets it plan to limit exposure.
perOption.c: Needed tests should not be delayed; safe transport is possible.
perOption.d: The client passes through hallways and elevators where others could be exposed.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.stem: A client has been on a mechanical ventilator for 3 days. Which measures should the nurse include to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed raised 30 to 45 degrees
Provide oral care and tooth brushing on a regular schedule
Change the ventilator circuit tubing every 24 hours
Take part in daily sedation interruptions and readiness-to-wean checks
Instill normal saline into the endotracheal tube before each suctioning

rationale.correct: VAP bundle: head of bed 30 to 45 degrees, oral care, daily sedation breaks and weaning checks; avoid routine saline instillation and unnecessary circuit changes.

perOption.a: Elevation reduces aspiration of stomach contents and oral secretions.
perOption.b: Oral care reduces bacteria in the mouth that can be aspirated.
perOption.c: Routine frequent circuit changes do not reduce pneumonia and add contamination risk; circuits are changed when soiled or damaged.
perOption.d: Shorter ventilation time lowers pneumonia risk.
perOption.e: Saline instillation can push bacteria deeper into the lungs.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.stem: The emergency department is told that several farm workers are being brought in after exposure to an organophosphate pesticide spray. They have wet clothing, drooling and pinpoint pupils. What should happen before the clients enter the department?

options.text: Remove the clients' clothing and decontaminate them with water outside the department
Give atropine to each client in the ambulance bay before decontamination
Place the clients in airborne isolation rooms in the main department as soon as they arrive
Ask the clients to shower at home first, then return for assessment

rationale.correct: Chemical exposures are decontaminated outside the department by staff in PPE before clients enter, to prevent secondary contamination.

perOption.a: Decontamination before entry protects staff and other clients from the chemical, which is absorbed through skin.
perOption.b: Atropine is needed, but staff must be protected; decontamination and PPE come first unless the facility has a treatment zone.
perOption.c: Airborne isolation does not address a chemical on the skin and clothing.
perOption.d: Sending exposed, symptomatic clients away is unsafe.

questions.stem: An 88-year-old client with dementia keeps pulling at an IV catheter that delivers antibiotics. The client is calm when family members are present. What should the nurse try first?

options.text: Ask the provider for an order for soft wrist restraints for the client's safety
Cover the IV site with a soft sleeve and invite the family to stay with the client
Give a dose of the prescribed as-needed sedative so the client sleeps through the antibiotic infusion
Remove the IV and give the antibiotic by intramuscular injection instead

rationale.correct: Try the least restrictive measures first: hide or protect devices, use family presence, distraction and frequent checks before restraints.

perOption.a: Restraints are a last resort after less restrictive measures have been tried.
perOption.b: Hiding the site and using a familiar person are less restrictive alternatives that often work.
perOption.c: Chemical restraint increases fall and delirium risk and is not a first measure.
perOption.d: Changing the route needs a prescription and may not be suitable for this antibiotic.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A small trash can fire starts in a client's room, and the nurse has already moved the client to safety, pulled the alarm and closed the door. Now the nurse gets a portable fire extinguisher. Place the steps for using the extinguisher in order.

items.text: Sweep the nozzle from side to side
Pull the pin on the extinguisher
Aim the nozzle at the base of the fire

rationale.correct: PASS: pull, aim at the base, squeeze, sweep. RACE comes first: rescue, alarm, contain, extinguish.

perOption.a: The pin keeps the handle from being squeezed.
perOption.b: The base is where the fuel burns.
perOption.c: Squeezing releases the agent.
perOption.d: Sweeping covers the whole base of the fire.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client who has never taken opioids before is admitted with a hip fracture. The prescription reads "hydromorphone 10 mg IV every 4 hours as needed for pain." The usual starting IV dose is 0.2 to 1 mg. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give 1 mg, since that is within the usual range, and document the change
Hold the dose and contact the prescriber to clarify the prescription
Give the 10 mg dose slowly over 10 minutes with naloxone at the bedside
Give morphine 10 mg instead, since it was probably meant to be morphine

rationale.correct: Hydromorphone and morphine are look-alike, sound-alike high-alert drugs; any dose far outside the usual range must be clarified before it is given.

perOption.a: Nurses may not change a dose; the prescription must be clarified.
perOption.b: A tenfold dose of a high-alert opioid in an opioid-naive client may be an error, perhaps confusion with morphine; it must be clarified first.
perOption.c: Giving it slowly does not prevent overdose from a possible tenfold error.
perOption.d: Substituting a drug without a prescription is outside the nurse's scope.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: During a safety round, the nurse checks the electrical equipment in a client's room. Highlight the findings that need action before the equipment is used.

cells: Power cord has tape wrapped around a cracked section
Plugged into a wall outlet with a three-prong plug
Brought from home with no safety inspection sticker
Plugged into a red emergency power outlet
Plugged into a household extension cord across the floor
Within the client's reach and working

rationale.correct: Remove equipment with damaged cords, check personal devices, avoid extension cords and keep essential devices on emergency power.

perOption.r1: Damaged cords can cause shocks or fires; the pump should be removed and sent for repair.
perOption.r3: Personal electrical devices usually need a safety check before use in the hospital.
perOption.r4: Essential equipment belongs on emergency power.
perOption.r5: Extension cords are a trip and electrical hazard.

questions.stem: At a 6-month well-baby visit, a breastfed infant can sit with support and opens their mouth when a spoon comes near. The parent describes plans for starting solids at home. Which plan needs to be corrected?

options.text: "I'll start with iron-fortified foods and offer one new food at a time, a few days apart."
"I'll add a little honey to the cereal so my baby is more willing to eat it."
"I'll keep breastfeeding while my baby learns to eat solids."
"I'll offer soft, mashed foods and watch for gagging or choking."

rationale.correct: No honey before 12 months (infant botulism); start iron-rich foods around 6 months, one new food at a time, while continuing breast milk or formula.

perOption.a: Iron-rich first foods and spacing new foods help find any food reactions.
perOption.b: Honey can cause infant botulism and is not given before 1 year of age.
perOption.c: Breast milk remains the main food in the first year.
perOption.d: Soft textures suit infants starting solids.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child is admitted for IV antibiotics and becomes very upset when the nurse approaches to check the IV site. Which approach is most appropriate for the child's developmental stage?

options.text: Explain the body's immune response in detail so the child understands why the IV is needed
Let the child put a bandage on a doll's "IV" before the nurse checks the child's own site
Check the site quickly while a parent holds the child down, without explaining first
Tell the child that the IV will be removed if they stop crying and sit still

rationale.correct: Preschoolers think magically and fear bodily harm; use simple words, medical play with dolls and give choices.

perOption.a: Detailed explanations are beyond a preschooler's thinking.
perOption.b: Preschoolers fear bodily injury; medical play lets them practice and gain a sense of control.
perOption.c: Surprise and restraint increase fear; short explanations and play help more.
perOption.d: Promises that may not be kept damage trust.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.educationalObjective: Use developmentally appropriate care for a preschooler.

questions.stem: At 28 weeks of gestation, the nurse reviews four prenatal clients' laboratory results. Which client should receive Rho(D) immune globulin today?

options.text: A client who is Rh-positive with a negative antibody screen and a partner who is Rh-negative
A client who is Rh-negative with a negative antibody screen and a partner whose Rh type is unknown
A client who is Rh-negative with a positive antibody screen for anti-D antibodies
A client who is Rh-negative with a negative antibody screen and a partner with confirmed Rh-negative blood

rationale.correct: Give Rho(D) immune globulin at 28 weeks and within 72 hours after birth to Rh-negative, unsensitized clients who may carry an Rh-positive fetus.

perOption.a: Rh-positive clients do not need Rho(D) immune globulin.
perOption.b: An Rh-negative, unsensitized client receives Rho(D) immune globulin at 28 weeks unless the fetus is known to be Rh-negative.
perOption.c: Once a client is already sensitized, Rho(D) immune globulin does not help; the pregnancy needs close monitoring.
perOption.d: If paternity is certain and the partner is Rh-negative, the fetus is Rh-negative and the injection is not needed.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify clients who need Rho(D) immune globulin.

questions.stem: A parent who is exclusively breastfeeding calls the clinic on the newborn's fifth day of life, worried that the baby is not getting enough milk. Which finding best shows that the newborn's intake is adequate?

options.text: The baby falls asleep after 5 minutes on the breast at most feedings
The baby has 6 or more wet diapers and several yellow stools each day
The baby nurses at 4- to 5-hour intervals and sleeps well between feedings
The parent's breasts feel full and heavy through the day, even right after feedings

rationale.correct: Adequate intake by day 5: 6 or more wet diapers, yellow stools, 8 to 12 feedings a day and weight gain after the early loss.

perOption.a: Falling asleep quickly can mean poor intake; it does not show the baby is getting enough.
perOption.b: By day 5, six or more wet diapers and yellow, seedy stools show good milk intake.
perOption.c: Newborns usually feed 8 to 12 times a day; long gaps can mean too little intake.
perOption.d: Breasts that stay full after feeding may mean milk is not being removed well.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a 79-year-old client at a wellness visit. For each finding, indicate whether it is an expected change of aging or should be reported for further evaluation.

rows.text: Gradual loss of the ability to hear high-pitched sounds
New forgetfulness that makes the client get lost driving home
Needing reading glasses for small print
Sudden loss of vision in one eye this morning
Taking longer to fall asleep and waking more often at night

rationale.correct: Gradual sensory and sleep changes are expected; sudden changes or memory loss that affects daily function need evaluation.

perOption.r1:c1: Presbycusis is a common, gradual change.
perOption.r2:c1: Getting lost in familiar places is not normal aging.
perOption.r2:c2: This may signal dementia or another problem and needs evaluation.
perOption.r3:c1: Presbyopia is expected after middle age.
perOption.r4:c1: Sudden vision loss is never normal aging.
perOption.r4:c2: This may be a retinal or vascular emergency.
perOption.r5:c1: Lighter, more broken sleep is common with aging.
perOption.r5:c2: This is usually expected, though sleep hygiene can help.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish normal aging from findings to report.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old client with a cervix has had normal cervical cytology (Pap) and human papillomavirus (HPV) co-testing results at ages 28 and 31, with no history of abnormal results. The client asks when the next screening is due. What should the nurse explain?

options.text: Screening is now due each year because the client is over 30 years old
The next co-test is due 5 years after the last one, at age 36
Screening can stop now, since there have been two normal results in a row
The client should switch to a Pap test alone at 2-year intervals from now on

rationale.correct: Cervical screening: cytology every 3 years from 21 to 29; from 30 to 65, co-testing or HPV testing alone every 5 years, or cytology every 3 years.

perOption.a: Yearly screening is not recommended for average-risk adults.
perOption.b: For ages 30 to 65 with normal results, co-testing every 5 years (or HPV testing alone every 5 years, or cytology every 3 years) is recommended.
perOption.c: Screening continues until 65 for most people with adequate normal results.
perOption.d: Every 2 years is not a recommended interval.

references: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client who smokes a pack a day says, "I know I should quit someday, and my kids keep asking me to, but I'm not ready yet." Which response best fits the client's stage of change?

options.text: "Let's set a quit date for next week and get you a nicotine patch prescription."
"What do you think you would gain if you quit, and what worries you about quitting?"
"Smoking will shorten your life, and you really need to stop now for your children's sake."
"Since you're not ready, we can talk about smoking again at next year's visit."

rationale.correct: In contemplation, clients see reasons to change but are ambivalent; motivational interviewing explores their own reasons.

perOption.a: Setting a quit date fits the preparation stage; this client is not ready to act.
perOption.b: The client is in contemplation; exploring the pros and cons builds motivation.
perOption.c: Lecturing and guilt tend to increase resistance.
perOption.d: Dropping the subject misses the chance to build motivation.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A parent asks why the newborn needs a vitamin K injection shortly after birth. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "It helps prevent bleeding, because newborns have low vitamin K levels at birth."
"It helps the newborn's eyes fight off infections picked up during birth."
"It protects the baby's liver from the hepatitis B virus in the first months."
"It lowers the bilirubin level so the baby is less likely to become jaundiced in the first week."

rationale.correct: Newborns receive vitamin K at birth to prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding, because their sterile gut cannot yet make it.

perOption.a: Newborns lack the gut bacteria that make vitamin K, so they are at risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding.
perOption.b: This describes erythromycin eye ointment.
perOption.c: This describes the hepatitis B vaccine.
perOption.d: Vitamin K does not prevent jaundice.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: A client at 26 weeks of gestation has a 1-hour 50 g glucose challenge test. The result is 152 mg/dL; the facility's cut-off is 140 mg/dL. Complete the sentence.

content.template: This result means the client {{b1}}, and the nurse should expect the provider to order {{b2}}.

options.text: needs further testing for gestational diabetes
has gestational diabetes and needs insulin
has a normal result for this stage of pregnancy
a 3-hour 100 g oral glucose tolerance test
a hemoglobin A1C next month
a repeat 1-hour test at 36 weeks

rationale.correct: Two-step screening: a positive 1-hour 50 g challenge is followed by a 3-hour 100 g glucose tolerance test to diagnose gestational diabetes.

perOption.b1:a: A result above the cut-off is a positive screen, not a diagnosis.
perOption.b1:b: A screening test alone does not diagnose gestational diabetes.
perOption.b1:c: 152 mg/dL is above the screening cut-off.
perOption.b2:a: The diagnostic test after a positive screen is the 3-hour glucose tolerance test.
perOption.b2:b: A1C is not used to diagnose gestational diabetes.
perOption.b2:c: Waiting would delay diagnosis and treatment.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
American Diabetes Association Standards of Care

questions.stem: A 52-year-old client with a long history of heavy alcohol use and poor nutrition is admitted with confusion. The client cannot walk without help because of a wide, unsteady gait, and the nurse notes jerky horizontal eye movements. The client is not tremulous, and the last drink was 3 days ago. A fingerstick glucose is 64 mg/dL. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

condition.text: Acute ischemic stroke of the cerebellum

actions.text: Give IV thiamine before any glucose-containing fluids
Put fall precautions in place and help the client with walking
Start an IV of 5% dextrose before the thiamine is available
Give a benzodiazepine on a fixed schedule for withdrawal
Restrict oral intake until the confusion clears

parameters.text: Blood pressure measured in both arms

rationale.correct: Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, nystagmus) is an emergency: give thiamine before glucose, protect from falls and watch mental status and eye and gait signs.

perOption.c1: Confusion, ataxia and nystagmus in a malnourished client with heavy alcohol use is Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency.
perOption.c2: Withdrawal delirium causes tremors, autonomic hyperactivity and hallucinations, not this triad.
perOption.c3: Stroke can cause ataxia, but the classic triad with alcohol use and malnutrition points to Wernicke.
perOption.c4: Hepatic encephalopathy causes confusion and asterixis, not nystagmus and ataxia.
perOption.a1: Glucose without thiamine can worsen Wernicke encephalopathy; thiamine comes first.
perOption.a2: Ataxia and confusion put the client at high risk of falls.
perOption.a3: Dextrose before thiamine can make the brain injury worse.
perOption.a4: The client shows no withdrawal signs; sedation adds fall risk.
perOption.a5: The client needs nutrition, given safely.
perOption.p1: Mental status shows whether thiamine is reversing the encephalopathy.
perOption.p2: Nystagmus and ataxia improve with thiamine and show response.
perOption.p3: Not a key sign of Wernicke encephalopathy.
perOption.p4: Lipase reflects the pancreas, not this condition.
perOption.p5: Not a key guide to this condition.

questions.stem: A client scheduled for a mastectomy in the morning is sitting on the bed wringing their hands and says, "I'm fine, I just can't stop thinking about tomorrow." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "You're in very good hands. The surgeon has done hundreds of these operations."
"You seem worried about tomorrow. What thoughts are going through your mind?"
"Would you like me to get you something to help you sleep tonight?"
"Try not to keep thinking about tomorrow. Watching a movie may help take your mind off it."

rationale.correct: Use observation and open-ended questions to explore anxiety; avoid false reassurance and changing the subject.

perOption.a: False reassurance closes the conversation.
perOption.b: Naming the observed feeling and asking an open question invites the client to share fears.
perOption.c: Offering medication sidesteps the client's feelings.
perOption.d: Distraction dismisses the client's concern.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client in an acute manic episode has lost 3 kg (6.6 lb) in a week, paces the unit constantly and will not sit down for meals. Which intervention best meets the client's nutritional needs?

options.text: Insist the client sit at the table with other clients until the meal is finished
Offer high-calorie finger foods and drinks the client can take while walking
Wait until the client feels hungry and asks for food on their own
Ask the dietitian for three large meals to be served in the client's room

rationale.correct: In mania, offer frequent high-calorie, high-protein finger foods and fluids that can be eaten on the move, in a low-stimulus setting.

perOption.a: A manic client cannot sit still, and a busy dining room is overstimulating.
perOption.b: Portable, high-calorie foods let the client eat without sitting still.
perOption.c: Clients in mania often ignore hunger and can become dangerously depleted.
perOption.d: Large meals that need sitting are unlikely to be eaten.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A veteran with post-traumatic stress disorder is admitted for knee surgery. During the night the nurse finds the client sweating and breathing fast after a nightmare. The client startles when the nurse touches their shoulder to wake them. Which approach best reflects trauma-informed care?

options.text: Turn on the overhead light and firmly shake the client's shoulder to wake them fully
Call the client's name from the doorway, then explain who you are before coming closer
Give the prescribed as-needed sedative so the client sleeps deeply through the night
Ask the client to describe the nightmare in detail so the nurse can document it in the record

rationale.correct: Trauma-informed care emphasizes safety, choice and control: announce yourself, ask before touching and avoid sudden actions.

perOption.a: Sudden light and touch can increase the sense of threat.
perOption.b: Announcing yourself and asking before touch gives the client a sense of safety and control.
perOption.c: Sedation does not address the response and may not be wanted.
perOption.d: Pushing for details can retraumatize the client.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with obsessive-compulsive disorder is admitted to a medical unit for pneumonia and spends long periods washing their hands. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Allow time for the hand-washing ritual at first, while setting limits on how long it lasts
Remove the soap and towels from the room so the client cannot keep washing
Plan care around the ritual so the client has time for treatments and meals
Check the skin of the hands for cracks and apply lotion
Tell the client that the washing is irrational and that it needs to stop today
Encourage the client to talk about feelings when anxiety builds

rationale.correct: In OCD, allow rituals at first with gradual limits, plan care around them, protect the skin and support other ways to manage anxiety.

perOption.a: Stopping rituals suddenly raises anxiety; limits are introduced gradually.
perOption.b: Taking away the means of the ritual causes severe anxiety.
perOption.c: Scheduling around the ritual makes sure essential care still happens.
perOption.d: Frequent washing damages skin and raises infection risk.
perOption.e: Clients usually know the ritual is excessive; arguing increases anxiety.
perOption.f: Talking about anxiety helps the client find other coping methods.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client comes to the emergency department with a broken wrist, saying they fell down stairs. The client's partner answers most questions and will not leave the room. The nurse notices bruises of different colors on the client's upper arms. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Ask the client in front of the partner whether anyone has been hurting them
Find a reason to see the client alone, such as an x-ray, and then ask about safety
Call the police to report the partner for domestic violence right away
Tell the partner that the injuries look like abuse and ask the partner for an explanation of them

rationale.correct: Screen for intimate partner violence in private, ask directly and without judgment, and plan for safety with the client.

perOption.a: Asking with the partner present can put the client in danger and is unlikely to get an honest answer.
perOption.b: Screening for violence is done privately, so the client can speak safely.
perOption.c: Most states do not require reporting adult partner violence without the client's agreement, and the client has not disclosed anything yet.
perOption.d: Confronting the partner can raise the risk of harm to the client.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: An 8-year-old child with autism spectrum disorder is admitted for surgery. The parent says the child becomes very upset by loud noises and changes in routine. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Place the child in a shared room near the nurses' station for close watching
Keep the child's home routine as much as possible and use a quiet private room
Introduce the child to the whole team at once so the child knows each person caring for them
Explain the surgery to the child in detail on the morning of the operation

rationale.correct: For children with autism: consistent routines and caregivers, a quiet environment, advance preparation and the parent's input.

perOption.a: A noisy shared room near the station is overstimulating.
perOption.b: Familiar routines and low stimulation reduce distress for children with autism.
perOption.c: Many new people at once is overwhelming; fewer consistent caregivers are better.
perOption.d: Preparing the child gradually with visual supports in advance works better.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: A client admitted with a myocardial infarction is found doing push-ups beside the bed and says, "It was just bad indigestion. There's nothing wrong with my heart." Which defense mechanism is the client using?

options.text: Denial
Projection
Displacement
Sublimation

rationale.correct: Denial protects against overwhelming news but can be dangerous when it leads to unsafe behavior after a cardiac event.

perOption.a: Refusing to accept the reality of the heart attack is denial.
perOption.b: Projection is putting one's own feelings onto someone else.
perOption.c: Displacement is redirecting feelings to a safer target.
perOption.d: Sublimation is channeling impulses into acceptable activities.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
